Amaltas Commerce: The Night Before the Product Council

Amaltas Commerce is a fictional company. The market, regulators, rails and brands named around it are real. Money is in ₹ lakh and ₹ crore.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

It was twenty minutes to midnight on Sunday, 16 November 2025, and Rukmini Iyer had stopped writing. She was at the dining table of her flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with three documents open: a six-slide deck for the product council at ten the next morning, a reconciliation spreadsheet from her analytics lead in Pune, and an email from Dubai that she had read four times and not answered.

The email was from Faisal Rahman, Vice-President Digital at the Zahra Group, a Gulf retail conglomerate that had put six of its brands onto Amaltas Commerce's storefront platform eighteen months earlier. Zahra's contract was worth ₹9.8 crore a year and came up for renewal on 31 December. Faisal's message ran to four lines. His team had reconciled Amaltas's Commerce Insights dashboard against Zahra's own payment records for the Ramadan and Eid campaigns and found that checkout starts differed by 14 per cent, orders by 6 per cent, and that the two numbers moved in opposite directions. "We are not accusing anyone of anything," he had written. "We are asking which number your platform believes, and why we should believe it."

Rukmini had been Chief Product Officer for fourteen months. She knew what she was going to be asked at ten o'clock, because the chief executive had already asked it twice: is our data broken, how much will it cost to fix, and does it stop the copilot? What she did not know was which of the four explanations on her table was true, or whether the question the board would ask was the right question at all. Her deck's title slide read "Single Source of Truth: A Two-Quarter Programme". She had been staring at the word "the" in "the truth" for some time.

2. How Amaltas got here, and the decision that still binds it

Amaltas Commerce was founded in Bengaluru in 2018 to sell the plumbing of Indian direct-to-consumer retail. By November 2025 it ran three products: Storefront, a hosted and white-label web and app commerce front end used by about 1,900 brands; Seller Studio, the console where brand teams managed catalogue, pricing and campaigns; and Amaltas Ops, an Android application used by pickers and dispatchers in roughly 240 warehouses and dark stores. Annual recurring revenue stood at ₹210 crore, growing 41 per cent, with 62 per cent from the long tail of small brands on self-serve plans and the rest from eleven enterprise accounts including Zahra.

The constraint that shaped everything came from March 2022. Amaltas was then adding eighty brands a month and had just been quoted ₹3.4 crore a year to keep its usage of a hosted product-analytics platform as volumes grew. Harsh Vardhan Sethi, the chief technology officer, made two decisions in the same week, and both were defensible at the time. First, Amaltas would move its event pipeline in-house, onto Kafka and ClickHouse, at an infrastructure cost that had since settled at about ₹2.1 crore a year. Second, instrumentation would be "squad-local": each squad would own, name and evolve its own events, because a central review would have become the bottleneck at the speed the company was shipping. The engineering blog post announcing this was still online and still quoted approvingly at conferences.

The consequence arrived a year later, and not through engineering. In April 2023 Amaltas launched Commerce Insights, a dashboard sold to brands as an add-on at ₹18,000 a month. It was a good product and 740 brands bought it, contributing about ₹16 crore of annual revenue. To close the first six enterprise deals, the sales team agreed to a schema appendix in the contract: a named list of events the platform would emit, with definitions, and a 99.5 per cent availability and accuracy commitment on the dashboard, backed by service credits. That appendix named add_to_cart, checkout_started, order_placed and eleven others. Squad-local naming had been an internal engineering preference. From April 2023, it was a contractual obligation whose vocabulary had been chosen by whichever squad happened to have written it first.

3. The industry around it

Indian D2C in 2025 was a market in which everybody's costs were somebody else's revenue. Brands sold simultaneously on their own Amaltas-powered storefronts, on Flipkart and Amazon, on Nykaa and Myntra for beauty and fashion, on Zepto and Swiggy Instamart for anything under ten minutes, and increasingly through ONDC-connected buyer apps. Payments moved on UPI through Razorpay and PhonePe's rails, with NPCI's mandate framework carrying subscription renewals. GST filings had to reconcile with order records. The Reserve Bank's tokenisation rules had already forced one round of checkout re-engineering.

ONDC mattered to this case more than its volume suggested. Amaltas had built an ONDC adapter in February 2024 so that brands on Storefront could receive orders from buyer apps on the network. The adapter was written by a small platform team against the protocol's own vocabulary — select, init, confirm, on_status — and its events were never mapped into the Storefront vocabulary, because at the time ONDC was believed to account for under 3 per cent of platform orders and nobody wanted to spend a sprint on it.

Two other forces bore down. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the rules that followed it had made Amaltas's legal counsel ask, in September, for an inventory of personal data in event properties; a sampling exercise found email addresses or phone numbers inside free-text properties on 41 event types, mostly in search and error payloads. And the company's own narrative had moved on: in the August investor update, the chief executive had promised an "AI merchandising copilot" for Q1 FY27 that would recommend pricing and assortment changes to brand teams. Everyone agreed the copilot needed trustworthy behavioural data. Nobody had yet written down what events a copilot would need that the platform did not already emit.

4. The situation in detail

What follows is the sequence as Rukmini had reconstructed it, together with what was believed at each point.

February 2024. ONDC adapter shipped. Belief: ONDC would stay marginal, so its events need not be mapped. What turned out to be wrong: by September 2025, ONDC accounted for 11 per cent of orders across the platform and 23 per cent for the four grocery brands, whose checkout funnels had therefore been missing a fifth of their volume for eighteen months.

September 2024. Amaltas Ops was rebuilt with an offline queue so that pickers in basements could keep working. Belief: the queue's retry logic was idempotent. What turned out to be wrong: one Android build, 4.8.2, reused a session-scoped identifier as the event identifier, so retries produced events that looked distinct.

March 2025. Jasleen Sahota, a data scientist in Toronto, noticed that dashboard gross merchandise value exceeded the finance ledger for most brands and wrote a de-duplication rule into the query layer, keyed on the event identifier. Belief: this corrected the over-count. Measured effect: platform-level GMV variance fell from 9.1 per cent to 3.4 per cent, and the matter was closed. What turned out to be wrong: because build 4.8.2 reused identifiers, the rule discarded legitimate distinct events from Ops, and because the rule ran at query time rather than in the pipeline, no record was kept of what it dropped.

July 2025. A mid-sized D2C brand, Brij Naturals, disputed a ₹44 lakh performance-marketing decision it said it had taken on the basis of Insights data, and asked for a credit. Customer success settled it quietly.

September to October 2025. Zahra Group ran its own reconciliation. Aparna Nadkarni, VP Analytics in Pune, ran a formal audit. Her audit found three causes and could not cleanly separate them. Meanwhile, the design team in Berlin shipped a Storefront beta that consolidated the cart and checkout screens — and, incidentally, removed two events whose names referred to the screens that no longer existed.

5. The people

Devika Raman, chief executive, Bengaluru. Position: the company needs "one source of truth" and the copilot must not slip, because the Series D conversation starts in February. Incentive: the growth narrative. Not saying: she has already told two prospective investors that Insights data is "audited", a word nobody inside the company has used.

Harsh Vardhan Sethi, chief technology officer, Bengaluru. Position: the data problem is real but a re-taxonomy is a six-quarter programme dressed as a two-quarter one, and the correct fix is a registry plus validation applied to new events only. Incentive: his own 2022 decision is implicitly on trial. Not saying: his platform team is down nine engineers after a difficult year of attrition, offers at Bengaluru senior-engineer bands of ₹70–95 lakh are being declined, and he cannot staff the programme he is being asked to cost.

Aparna Nadkarni, VP Analytics, Pune. Position: nothing improves until there is a canonical event spine with required identifiers, a schema registry and CI enforcement; the mapping layer is a liability, not a solution. Incentive: her team absorbs the blame for every disputed number. Not saying: the 1,100-line mapping layer is hers, is undocumented, and the only other engineer who understands it resigned on 4 November with a last working day of 28 November.

Meghna Pillai, head of customer success, Singapore. Position: whatever is done must not change what brands see in their dashboards, because 740 of them have built their own reporting on top of it and six have it in a contract. Incentive: renewals and net revenue retention, which is her bonus line. Not saying: she has issued ₹64 lakh of service credits across eleven accounts in the past two quarters under a discretionary limit, and has not escalated the pattern.

Jasleen Sahota, data scientist, Toronto. Position: the March correction was right in direction and she now believes it over-corrected for Ops events; she wants two weeks to quantify it properly. Incentive: she is the author of the rule. Not saying: she cannot reproduce the March analysis, because the intermediate table it ran on was dropped in a June storage clean-up, and her notebook references a column that no longer exists.

Tobias Lang, principal designer, Berlin. Position: the Storefront redesign has been committed to three enterprise logos for January and cannot wait for an instrumentation programme. Incentive: the redesign is his year's work. Not saying: the beta already in production for 40 brands removed cart_page_viewed and checkout_step_2_viewed, both of which appear in the contractual schema appendix, and he did not know the appendix existed.

Vivek Ramaswamy, head of enterprise sales, New Jersey. Position: conversion analytics is the differentiator in every US deal he is running, including one with a listed speciality retailer worth ₹12 crore a year; anything that pauses Insights development costs him the quarter. Incentive: his pipeline. Not saying: he has shown two prospects a demo dashboard populated with numbers drawn from the pre-March methodology.

Faisal Rahman, VP Digital, Zahra Group, Dubai. Position: he wants a reconciliation, a stated definition for every metric on his dashboard, and an explanation of the 14 per cent gap before he signs a renewal. Incentive: he defended the choice of Amaltas internally against a global platform and his own credibility is attached to it. Not saying: Zahra's internal figures are compiled from a payment gateway that reports in Gulf Standard Time on a Sunday-start week, while Amaltas reports in IST on a Monday-start week — which his own analyst mentioned once, in a footnote, and nobody pursued.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

What I did not anticipate is that sales would put our internal event names into a contract. That is not an instrumentation failure. And before anyone costs a 148-week programme: I have nine open roles and two offers declined last month."
Aparna Nadkarni — Slack, #data-platform, 5 November, 11:42 p.m. IST"Every quarter we agree the mapping layer is temporary and every quarter it grows. It is now the actual definition of our contracted product. If I get hit by a bus on the way to Hinjewadi, Commerce Insights becomes an unmaintainable 1,100-line query. Kabir's last day is the 28th."

Please understand what 'properly' looks like from my side: 740 brands have built their own Google Sheets and Looker reports on top of our numbers. The day our numbers change, every one of those breaks, and they will not read our change note. Last quarter I settled eleven of these conversations. I would rather a consistent number that is slightly wrong than a correct number that arrives as a surprise."

I can rebuild the analysis on current data but then I'm not comparing like with like, and I'd rather say that out loud than have it in a board deck as a fact."

Vivek Ramaswamy — call with Rukmini, 14 November, 8:00 a.m. EST"In the US, everyone I sell to already has a data team that will pull our numbers apart in week two. Insights is why we win. If the answer on Monday is that we pause Insights for two quarters to rebuild plumbing, I need to know today, because I have two deals where I have been showing conversion dashboards."
Faisal Rahman — email, 16 November, 7:12 p.m. GST"To be clear, we are not asking for a credit. We are asking for a definition. Send me, for each of the six metrics on our dashboard, the events it is built from, the moment each fires, the timezone, and the week convention. If the answer is that these definitions do not exist in written form, that is also an answer, and we will plan accordingly."

8. The options as Rukmini sees them

Her deck has three.

Option A — build the canonical spine. Define a platform-wide event vocabulary with required identifiers (order, brand, session, actor), a schema registry, codegen and CI enforcement; re-emit across all five emitters; migrate Insights onto it with dual running. Costed at ₹280–360 lakh, somewhere between 86 and 148 engineering weeks depending on whom one believes, and it displaces the Storefront redesign committed to three January logos. Rukmini's note to herself beside this option reads: right answer, wrong calendar, and the estimate range is itself evidence that nobody knows the scope.

Option B — formalise the semantic layer. Leave emission alone. Take Aparna's 1,100 lines, rewrite them as reviewed, tested, version-controlled models with documented definitions, publish those definitions to customers, and staff it properly before Kabir leaves on 28 November. ₹58–74 lakh, roughly six weeks. It answers Faisal's actual question — what is the definition — without touching a single client release. It does not create the order-level identifier that the ONDC adapter never emitted, so grocery brands' funnels remain structurally incomplete, and it leaves the meaning of the product inside a modelling layer rather than in the platform.

Option C — change the contract, not the code. Renegotiate the schema appendix out of the six enterprise contracts at the next renewal, replacing named events with service-level commitments on the dashboard's availability and a defined change-notice process; take the credits; defer the engineering. ₹12 lakh plus whatever the credits cost. It buys eighteen months of freedom for design and platform. It also means telling Faisal, six weeks before a ₹9.8 crore renewal, that Amaltas would like to remove the clause he relies on.

Rukmini has written, in the margin of the last slide, three sentences she has not decided whether to say aloud. The first: none of these three options mentions the copilot, which is the only thing the board actually cares about, and the copilot needs events we do not emit at all — what a brand team did with a recommendation, and whether it worked. The second: Exhibit 2 says our problem has two opposite signs, and all three options treat it as one problem. The third: if the question is "can we build funnels and cohorts later", then the thing we are missing is not a vocabulary. It is an order identifier that survives across four emitters, and a written definition of when each event fires. We could have both without renaming anything.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The product council meets at ten on Monday, 17 November, and Devika has asked for a recommendation, a cost and a date, not for options. Zahra's renewal falls on 31 December, and Faisal has asked for definitions, not for a programme. Kabir Menon, the second maintainer of the mapping layer, leaves on 28 November, after which the layer has one person who understands it and she is in Pune with a team of nine covering all analytics for the company. Harsh has nine unfilled engineering roles and a hiring market in which Bengaluru senior offers at ₹70–95 lakh are being declined; contract engineers can be brought in at roughly ₹2.6 lakh a month per head but need eight weeks to become useful in the pipeline codebase. The Storefront redesign is contractually promised to three enterprise accounts for January, worth ₹18 crore in aggregate. The DPDP inventory must be delivered to counsel by 31 December, and the 41 event types carrying personal data in free-text properties will need either scrubbing at emission or a defensible rationale. The ClickHouse bill is ₹2.1 crore a year and the chief financial officer in Mumbai has asked, separately and inconveniently, whether returning to a hosted analytics platform would now be cheaper than staffing the alternative. Amaltas's cash position supports about ₹4 crore of unbudgeted spend this fiscal year without a conversation with the board, and the Series D conversation begins in February.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Working only from Exhibits 1 to 4, what can be established about the sources of the variance, and what cannot? Which exhibit would you refuse to put in front of the board in its present form, and why?

2. Exhibit 2 shows variances of opposite sign in different segments while the platform total is under 1 per cent. What does that pattern rule out, and what does it suggest about where to look first?

3. The March 2025 de-duplication rule reduced the headline variance and closed the issue. Evaluate that decision on the information available in March, and then on the information available now. What, procedurally, would have caught the problem earlier?

4. The 2022 squad-local instrumentation decision is defended by the person who made it and blamed by nearly everyone else. Separate the decision from its consequences: which of today's problems follow from squad-local naming, and which follow from later choices such as putting event names into a customer contract?

5. Each of the eight stakeholders is holding something back. For three of them, describe how what they are not saying changes the option you would otherwise recommend, and what Rukmini would have to do to surface it before Monday.

6. What should Rukmini do on Monday morning, and what exactly should she say to the board — including what she would commit to, what she would refuse to commit to, and what she would tell them she does not yet know? If you believe her three options are the wrong three, say what the fourth is and what it costs.

At half past midnight, Rukmini did two things. She wrote a reply to Faisal — "Sending you written definitions for all six metrics by Wednesday, with the timezone and week convention stated for each; some of them do not exist in written form today and I would rather tell you that than guess" — and left it in drafts. Then she opened the deck, deleted the title slide, and typed a new one. She got as far as What we know, what we don't, and before she stopped, because she did not know how the sentence ended, and because the honest version of the third clause was a question about whether the company had spent three years measuring the wrong things carefully. The cursor blinked. Outside, on 12th Main, the last of the Diwali lights from the previous month were still strung across the balcony opposite, unlit.

Designing an Event Taxonomy

Are our events named and structured so we can build funnels and cohorts later? It sounds like housekeeping. It is a design decision that either enables every analysis a company will want to run, or quietly forecloses most of them.

1. A dashboard that would not add up

On the morning of 11 March 2024, Kabir Anand, head of product at Gulmohar Foods, a Bengaluru quick-commerce grocery app operating in six cities, opened a retention dashboard his data team had spent three weeks building and found two numbers that could not both be true. The checkout funnel showed 41,200 users starting checkout in the last week of February and 38,900 completing an order — a 94 percent completion rate that would have made Gulmohar the envy of every grocery app in the country. The revenue ledger for the same week, reconciled against payment-gateway settlements, showed 24,600 completed orders. Someone, somewhere, was double-counting.

The cause, once his data lead Meera Iyer traced it, was almost embarrassing. Gulmohar's Android app logged the successful purchase as order_placed. The iOS app, built by a different squad eighteen months earlier, logged the same moment as Order Completed. A third event, checkout_success, had been added by the payments team during a UPI-retry redesign and fired every time a retried payment succeeded — including retries within the same order, so one grocery order paid for on the third attempt could register as three successes. The funnel tool, built to be forgiving, counted all three names as evidence of a purchase. Nobody had lied or even been careless in any single decision; three teams, over three years, had each named the thing in front of them in the way that made sense to them at the time.

The stakes were not abstract. Gulmohar was six weeks from a board review at which the growth team wanted to argue for a ₹40 crore marketing push into two new cities, justified by a claimed 68 percent week-two retention cohort. If that cohort number was built on the same kind of event drift, Kabir would be asking the board to fund expansion on a number nobody could defend under questioning. He had two choices: patch the dashboard with a one-off SQL fix before the board meeting, or stop and design an event taxonomy — a shared, governed vocabulary for what gets logged and how — before anyone built another funnel on the mess. He chose the second, and the board meeting moved by three weeks.

2. The idea, plainly stated

An event taxonomy is the naming and structuring system a product team agrees on for the discrete user actions and system occurrences it logs for analysis — what each event is called, what properties travel with it, and what distinguishes one event from a merely similar one. It is not the analytics tool. Amplitude, Mixpanel, Segment and Google Analytics 4 are places a taxonomy gets executed; the taxonomy itself is a design document, a set of conventions that could in principle be written on paper before a line of tracking code exists.

The problem it solves is older than any of those tools. Web analytics teams in the mid-2000s, in a discipline still finding its footing, discovered that raw clickstream logs were nearly useless for business questions because the same user action was captured inconsistently across pages and releases. The customer-data-platform vendor Segment popularised a formal answer around 2015 with its "tracking plan" convention: name events as an Object followed by a past-tense Verb — Order Completed, Cart Viewed, Signup Started — and treat properties as adjectives describing that event, never as new events of their own. That grammar caught on because it forced a discipline ad-hoc logging never had: before anyone writes a tracking call, someone has to decide what counts as one event, what varies within it, and what its lifecycle looks like start to finish.

The single sentence Kabir could repeat in a board meeting without sounding glib is this:

If two things could mean the same user action, they must share the same event name — and if one thing could mean two different actions, it needs two.

Everything a taxonomy does is an application of that sentence, applied methodically across every screen, platform and team that touches the product.

3. The mechanics, walked through

Practitioners who are good at this move through five steps, and the two most often skipped are the first and the last.

Step one: enumerate the actions that matter, not the actions that are easy to log. Meera's team began in a whiteboard session with product, growth and the two mobile leads, listing every moment in the ordering journey a future funnel or cohort might need: app opened, search performed, item added to cart, checkout started, payment attempted, order placed, order delivered, order cancelled. Eleven events, far fewer than the fifty-odd tracking calls already scattered through both codebases, since most of those fifty logged implementation detail — button taps, screen renders — rather than user intent.

Step two: fix a naming grammar and apply it without exception. Gulmohar adopted Object-Verb-Past-Tense: Order Placed, Cart Item Added, Checkout Started. Every existing variant — order_placed, Order Completed, checkout_success — was mapped to exactly one canonical name, kept as a living document, not folklore in someone's head.

Step three: separate what makes an event distinct (a new event) from what merely describes it (a property). Payment method — UPI, card, wallet, cash-on-delivery — is not four different purchase events; it is one property, payment_method, attached to one Order Placed event. This is the step teams under deadline pressure skip most, because splitting by property feels like preserving more information, when it actually multiplies the number of event names a future analyst must know about and union together.

Step four: decide what identifies "the same event" across platforms and across a retry. This is the implicit step that caused Gulmohar's original bug. A retried UPI payment that eventually succeeds is one order, so the taxonomy needed an explicit rule: Order Placed fires exactly once per successful order, keyed to a server-generated order ID, never to a client-side payment attempt. Retries get their own event, Payment Retry Attempted, useful for a different analysis but never to be confused with a purchase.

Step five: assign an owner, a review process and a version. Every Gulmohar event now has a named owner accountable for its correctness, a changelog entry, and a rule that no new event ships without a fifteen-minute review against the existing list, to catch a proposed CartAdd before it duplicates the existing Cart Item Added.

4. A funnel, built and rebuilt

Meera rebuilt the checkout funnel for the last week of February using the new taxonomy, with Order Placed deduplicated to one row per order_id. Corrected: 41,200 users triggered Checkout Started; 33,760 reached Payment Attempted at least once; 24,600 produced exactly one Order Placed. Checkout-to-payment conversion was 33,760 / 41,200 = 81.9 percent. Payment-to-order conversion was 24,600 / 33,760 = 72.9 percent. Overall completion was 24,600 / 41,200 = 59.7 percent — not the fictitious 94 percent, but a number the payments team could act on, since a 27-point drop between attempt and completion pointed squarely at UPI failures, not checkout UX.

The second pass tested one changed input: what if a payments fix cut failed-then-retried payments in half? Moving half of the roughly 9,160 users who succeeded only on a retry into a first-attempt success lifted payment-to-order conversion from 72.9 percent to roughly 84 percent, and overall completion to about 68.8 percent — a nine-point gain from a payments engineering fix, not a marketing spend, visible only because the funnel could now be trusted stage by stage rather than read as one suspicious headline number.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Events and properties are often confused, and the confusion compounds

The most common early mistake is creating a new event for every variant of an action — Cart Item Added From Search, Cart Item Added From Recommendation — instead of one event, Cart Item Added, with a source property. Each extra event is a new thing every future analyst must remember exists and remember to include in a funnel. Properties scale; event names do not.

Granularity has no universally correct answer, only a correct answer for the questions being asked

A taxonomy built for funnel analysis wants coarse, intent-level events; one built to debug a specific screen wants finer-grained interaction events. Gulmohar kept both, in different tiers with different retention policies — core business events kept indefinitely, granular UI events pruned after ninety days — rather than pretending one list could serve both purposes equally well.

Identity stitching is a taxonomy problem before it is an engineering problem

A funnel is only as good as the certainty that the same person is tracked from step one to step four. Gulmohar's anonymous web sessions were not reliably merged with logged-in app sessions until the taxonomy explicitly defined an identity-resolution rule: device ID pre-login, user ID post-login, merged at sign-in. Without that rule stated up front, cohort sizes silently shrink or duplicate.

Versioning is not optional once the product changes

When Gulmohar added a "save for later" feature, checkout gained a step, and Checkout Started quietly meant something slightly different before and after the release. A taxonomy needs a version marker or a documented change date, or historical funnels silently misrepresent what happened.

A taxonomy cannot tell you why, only what and how often

Even a flawless taxonomy tells Kabir that 27 percent of payment attempts failed to convert; it does not say whether that is a UPI-app timeout, a bank decline, or hesitation at the final screen. Causal explanation needs either qualitative research or a deliberately designed property such as failure_reason, captured at the moment of failure — or the question stays unanswerable after the fact.

It is routinely confused with "having an analytics tool installed"

Installing Amplitude or Mixpanel does not produce a taxonomy any more than buying a filing cabinet produces an organised filing system. Many teams discover, as Gulmohar did, that they paid for sophisticated tooling for two years while feeding it ungoverned, duplicative event names the whole time.

Over-instrumentation is a real cost, not a safety margin, and discipline still depends on implementation

Logging everything "in case it's useful later" produces catalogues with hundreds of near-duplicate names nobody can audit, inflates warehouse cost, and buries the one correct event. Step one's discipline prevents this — but even the best-designed spec fails if an engineer under deadline pressure ships a new event without checking it; the review step is what keeps the taxonomy from decaying back into the mess Kabir found.

6. How this differs by product type and by company stage

In a consumer app like Gulmohar, the taxonomy centres on a single, well-worn purchase or engagement journey repeated by millions of similar users, so the payoff is tight standardisation of a short core list and heavy investment in identity stitching across app and web. In a B2B product, the taxonomy must represent both individual user actions and account-level events — a Report Exported action belongs to a user, but "this account renewed" is an account-level event a person-level taxonomy will not capture unless it is explicitly designed to roll up. In a marketplace — Gulmohar's own delivery-partner side — two taxonomies sit in tension: buyer-side events like Order Placed and supply-side events like Delivery Accepted, which must share a common order ID if anyone wants to answer a cross-side question such as how rider acceptance time affects buyer conversion the following week.

Company stage matters as much as product type. An early-stage team of six, moving fast with one codebase, can hold the whole event list in a shared spreadsheet and enforce discipline through a weekly stand-up; the cost of a loose taxonomy is low because little historical data rides on it. Gulmohar, three years and two platforms in, had crossed the threshold where informal discipline stops working. Past that threshold, the taxonomy needs a formal schema registry, an owner for governance — increasingly a "data product manager" role — and an automated validation step in the release pipeline that rejects a new event name not on the approved list: the same problem, solved with proportionally more process.

7. Common mistakes, and how to catch them cheaply

Synonym explosion. Symptom: a funnel showing implausibly high conversion, as Gulmohar's did. Misunderstanding: treating "we logged something" as equivalent to "we logged the same thing consistently." Cheapest diagnostic: query the raw event table for distinct names sharing a root word — "order," "checkout," "buy" — and see how many variants surface before trusting any funnel built on that action.

Event-property confusion. Symptom: an event list that keeps growing every sprint faster than the product does. Misunderstanding: treating a variant as a new occurrence rather than a description of one occurrence. Cheapest diagnostic: for any two similarly named events, ask whether one property could distinguish them; if yes, they should be one event.

No identity rule. Symptom: cohort sizes that do not reconcile with known user counts, usually under-counting. Misunderstanding: assuming the analytics tool resolves identity automatically. Cheapest diagnostic: pick fifty known repeat customers and check whether their pre- and post-login events are stitched into one profile.

No ownership. Symptom: an event that quietly stops firing after a refactor, unnoticed for months. Misunderstanding: treating instrumentation as a one-time build rather than a maintained asset. Cheapest diagnostic: for each core event, ask who would be paged if it stopped firing tomorrow — if the honest answer is nobody, there is no real owner.

8. What good looks like

Six months after the board review, Kabir's team could answer a request from a new growth hire — retention for users acquired through the Hosur Road dark-store launch, split by first-order coupon use — inside a single working day, using self-serve cohort tools built directly on the governed event list, without one ad-hoc SQL patch. The event dictionary lived in a shared document with forty-one approved events, each with an owner, a one-line definition, required properties, and a "last verified firing correctly" date. New events went through a fifteen-minute weekly review with one PM and one engineer from each platform team. When payments wanted a new retry-tracking event eight months later, the review caught that it overlapped 80 percent with an existing one and the team amended a property instead of shipping a duplicate. Nobody in that room thought of it as taxonomy work anymore; it was simply how Gulmohar shipped.

9. What Kabir decided, and what comes next

Kabir did not present the corrected 59.7 percent completion rate as bad news at the delayed board meeting. He presented it as the first trustworthy number Gulmohar had ever produced for that funnel, alongside the payments-fix scenario showing a defensible path to 68.8 percent through engineering investment rather than the original ₹40 crore marketing ask. The board approved a smaller, staged expansion, contingent on the payments fix shipping first — a more modest outcome than the original pitch, but built on numbers that would survive an audit.

The natural next things to learn, in order, are telemetry requirements (what must be true about the pipeline — latency, completeness, reliability — for a taxonomy to be worth designing at all), metric definitions and data quality (how a well-named event becomes a well-defined metric with an owner and a cadence), and constructing a funnel properly once the underlying events can be trusted. Each depends on the taxonomy being right first; building any of them on Gulmohar's original mess would only have produced a more sophisticated way to be wrong.

Two questions worth sitting with: First, in your own product, if you queried the raw event table for every event name containing the word "purchase," "signup," or "complete," how many variants would come back — and would you be surprised? Second, for the single most business-critical event your team tracks, who is the named owner, and what would that person actually be told if the event silently stopped firing next Tuesday?

Kavach Insure: Three Surfaces, One Funnel

A teaching case on designing an event taxonomy. Kavach Insure is a fictional company; the market, regulators and brands around it are real.

1. Friday evening, Lower Parel

At a quarter past eight on Friday, 3 October 2025, the twelfth-floor office of Kavach Insure in Lower Parel, Mumbai, had emptied except for the growth pod and Ananya Bhatt, its Vice-President of Product. On the whiteboard behind her was a single line, written that morning and not yet erased: Motor renewal push — 13 Oct to 22 Oct — ₹6.4 crore of premium at stake. Diwali fell on 20 October. The festive fortnight was when Indians bought and insured two-wheelers and cars, and Kavach had one clean shot at it.

The difficulty was not the campaign. It was that Ananya had spent the week trying to establish a baseline for it and had failed. Kavach sold through three surfaces — its own consumer app, an embedded software development kit installed inside partners' checkout flows, and a web console used by its network of 4,100 point-of-sale agents — and each surface described the same customer journey in a different vocabulary. The chief executive, Prithvi Ranade, had asked for a number at the Monday review: of customers who saw a renewal quote, what share paid? Ananya could produce three numbers, none of which could be added together.

She had until Monday, 6 October, to choose what to do, and until roughly 11 October to have anything shipped. Whatever she chose would also have to survive the renewal of the Marhaba Trips contract in Dubai, due on 30 November and worth ₹3.1 crore a year, because Marhaba's product head had begun asking for conversion reporting that Kavach could not currently produce for a partner surface.

2. Kavach Insure

Kavach Insure was founded in Mumbai in 2019 by two insurance executives and an engineer, on a simple observation: Indians bought insurance at the moment they bought something else. Registered with the IRDAI as a corporate agent and later as a web aggregator, Kavach did not underwrite risk. It distributed motor, health and travel policies from a panel of eleven insurers and earned commission, at an annualised gross written premium of ₹640 crore and revenue of ₹92 crore in FY25.

The market it operated in was crowded and well capitalised. Policybazaar dominated search-led comparison; Acko and Digit had built digital-first underwriting; Turtlemint had gone deep on the advisor network. Kavach's wedge was embedding: its SDK sat inside the checkout of a two-wheeler retail chain, a bus-ticketing app, and Marhaba Trips, a Dubai-based travel marketplace selling to the Gulf's Indian diaspora. Payments ran over UPI and cards through Razorpay; renewals were collected by UPI Autopay mandates on the NPCI rails. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, had recently made the legal team considerably more interested in what the product logged.

The three surfaces had been built in three different years by three different teams, and that history was the whole of Ananya's problem. The consumer app (2020) was instrumented by an Android team in Bengaluru using screen-based event names. The agent console (2021) was instrumented by a backend team in Pune that logged database state transitions. The SDK (2023) had been built fast for a partner deadline, with event names chosen to match that first partner's own analytics vocabulary — and then shipped, unchanged, to every partner since.

3. The situation

Ananya's week had produced Exhibit 1, an inventory that Aditi Raghunathan, Kavach's data scientist in Toronto, had assembled by querying the raw event store. It listed, for each stage of the renewal journey, what each surface actually emitted and whether it could be joined to the others.

First, the SDK's txnComplete fired when the partner's own checkout completed, which for Marhaba Trips included the flight booking whether or not travel insurance was attached — so the single most-used event in the partner funnel did not mean what its name implied. Second, the app's pay_btn_tap fired on the tap, not on the payment, and September's tap count exceeded the issued-policy count by a factor of 2.6, which the growth pod had been reading as price sensitivity. Third, nothing in the app or the SDK carried a renewal-opportunity identifier, so a customer who saw a quote in the app and later renewed through an agent appeared as two unrelated people.

Aditi's view, sent as a note at 6 a.m. Toronto time, was blunt: "I can model around messy names. I cannot model a field that was never captured. Three of the five stages have no joinable identifier, and no amount of SQL will create one retrospectively." Lukas Brenner, the designer in Berlin, saw it from a different angle: he had redesigned the quote screen twice in 2025, and both times the funnel had broken because the event names were screen names. Serene Tan, the customer-success lead in Singapore who managed the SDK partners, wanted a taxonomy she could publish to partners as a document, because she was tired of explaining that Kavach's own dashboard and the partner's dashboard disagreed.

4. The people

Prithvi Ranade, chief executive, Mumbai. Wants one credible quote-to-paid number for the board's product committee and for a Series C conversation in January. Is unsentimental about engineering elegance and deeply unsentimental about missing the festive fortnight.

Karthik Iyengar, engineering lead for the consumer app, Bengaluru. Estimates three weeks of team time to re-instrument the app properly, and points out that 26 per cent of Kavach's users are on an app build more than four months old, so any new event takes six to eight weeks to reach most users regardless of how fast his team writes it.

Shreya Deshmukh, engineering lead for the SDK and platform, Pune. Argues that the SDK cannot be changed unilaterally: every partner integration is a contract, and a new SDK version requires the partner's own release cycle. Marhaba Trips releases once a month; the bus-ticketing partner, twice a year.

Aditi Raghunathan, data scientist, Toronto. Wants required identifiers and two timestamps on every event, and is willing to live with ugly names. Her working hours overlap Mumbai's only in the Indian evening, which has made her the person who discovers data breakages overnight and reports them at standup.

Serene Tan, customer-success lead, Singapore. Owns the partner relationships including Marhaba Trips, whose product head in Dubai has asked for a monthly attach-rate report. Wants a published, stable event contract she can hand to partners without a caveat.

The arithmetic that made Prithvi uncomfortable was simple. Kavach could measure the funnel for the surface carrying 27 per cent of premium and not for the two carrying 73 per cent. The festive campaign would spend ₹1.9 crore on performance marketing and agent incentives across all three, and at the end of it the company would be able to say what happened on one of them.

5. The options

Option A: the full re-taxonomy. Freeze feature work, design a canonical event vocabulary for all three surfaces, re-instrument everything, publish a partner contract. Karthik and Shreya jointly estimate six to seven weeks and roughly ₹48 lakh of engineering cost, and it cannot be complete before January because of app adoption and partner release cycles. Upside: one vocabulary, permanently. Cost: the festive fortnight is measured no better than last year, and the roadmap slips past the Series C conversation.

Option B: a canonical spine for the renewal funnel only. Define fourteen events covering the five journey stages, in an object–action grammar with a required renewal_opportunity_id, policy_id and two timestamps. Ship it in the app immediately, add it server-side for the console (where no client release is needed, and therefore where it works instantly), and emit it in the next SDK version for partners to adopt at their own pace, keeping the legacy names alive in parallel with a mapping table. Estimated three weeks, about ₹19 lakh. Upside: the two surfaces Kavach controls are measurable during the campaign, and the identifier that cannot be created retrospectively starts being captured now. Cost: partial coverage for a quarter; two vocabularies coexisting; the other 169 event names untouched.

Option C: fix it in the warehouse. Leave emission alone; have Aditi build a mapping layer in the warehouse that aliases the three vocabularies into one model and infers the missing stages from the transaction database. Estimated one week, about ₹4 lakh, no release dependency. Upside: something exists before the campaign starts, and it is revisable. Cost: it cannot invent the joinable identifier, so cross-surface journeys stay invisible; the meaning lives in one analyst's models in a different timezone; and Serene has nothing she can publish to Marhaba Trips.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 disagree about what Kavach can measure. Working only from the case, which single missing field does the most damage to the company's ability to build funnels and cohorts, and why?

2. Why did three competent teams produce three vocabularies? Identify the decisions — technical, organisational and commercial — that made each naming scheme locally reasonable.

3. Karthik's app adoption lag and Shreya's partner release cycles are different kinds of constraint. How should each change Ananya's sequencing, as distinct from her design?

4. Which option would you choose on Monday 6 October, and what exactly would you tell Prithvi to expect from the ₹1.9 crore campaign? What would you deliberately choose not to measure this quarter?

7. A note for the learner

This decision looks like an engineering prioritisation and is in fact a taxonomy design problem. An event taxonomy is the agreed vocabulary and structure of a product's behavioural record: which actions are logged, what each is called, what properties travel with it, and which identifiers join events to a person, a policy or an account. The useful test is the one Aditi applies — not "are the names tidy?" but "can a question nobody anticipated be answered from this log later, without re-instrumenting?"

Two asymmetries organise a good answer. The first is that names can be repaired retrospectively and identifiers cannot. Aliasing offerShown to quote_shown in the warehouse is a morning's work, and can be back-dated over all of history. A renewal-opportunity identifier that was never emitted is gone for every event already written. That argues for spending the scarce eight days on capturing fields, not on renaming things. The second is that the surfaces differ in how fast a change reaches users. Server-side events for the agent console take effect on deployment; app events take six to eight weeks to reach most devices; SDK events wait on someone else's release calendar. A design that treats the three identically will be right about the vocabulary and wrong about the timeline.

A well-reasoned answer will also notice that two of the case's numbers are not what they appear. The app's 7.5 per cent quote-to-paid rate is computed from an event that fires on a tap, so the true rate is higher and the "price sensitivity" story is partly an artefact of the firing moment. The SDK's 11,60,000 quotes counts offers that rendered, not offers that were seen, which flatters the denominator and would make any partner attach rate look worse than it is. Both are firing-moment problems, and both are fixed by definition rather than by effort.

One defensible path. Ananya takes Option B, with Option C's mapping layer as its first week of work rather than as an alternative. Concretely: by Monday she publishes fourteen event definitions in object–action grammar with renewal_opportunity_id, policy_id, surface, occurred_at and received_at required on every one, and with intent and outcome separated (renewal_quote_shown, renewal_payment_started, policy_issued). The console version ships server-side by 9 October, giving her the surface with ₹17.3 crore of premium immediately. The app version ships in the 11 October build, acknowledging it will cover perhaps half of users during the campaign. Aditi's mapping layer aliases the legacy names so that a single funnel exists on 13 October, imperfect and documented as such. The SDK emits the new events in its November version; Serene gets a two-page contract to send to Marhaba Trips before the 30 November renewal, and Rajiv gets something to sell rather than something to promise. Legacy names are deprecated, not deleted, with dual emission for six weeks and a reconciliation report before anything is switched off.

The reasoning is that Ananya's binding constraint is a calendar she does not control, and her irreversible loss is uncaptured identifiers. Option A is the right design executed against the wrong clock; Option C is the right clock with a permanent hole in the middle. Option B accepts partial coverage for one quarter in exchange for a contract that is real, published and enforceable — and it tells Prithvi the honest thing, which is that the festive fortnight will be measured well on 60 per cent of premium and estimated on the rest.

Designing an Event Taxonomy

A taxonomy is not a naming convention. It is a set of commitments — about grain, identity, coverage and time — made before anyone knows which questions will be asked, and it can be scored.

1. Two rooms, three weeks apart

On 14 August 2025, in Pune, Arundhati Rao asked her data lead for something she believed was routine. Rao was VP Product at Suchipatra Clinical Systems, which sold revenue-cycle and clinical-documentation software to 240 hospital accounts and booked ₹186 crore of annual recurring revenue. Seventy-one of those accounts, worth ₹52 crore, renewed within nine months, and the chief executive wanted a product-usage health score for each before the sales plan was locked.

Nandan Bhide came back four days later. The event store held 4.1 billion rows and could not produce the score. Events were grained to the person; the contract was grained to the facility. The property facility_id appeared on 63 percent of events, and the missing 37 percent was not a random sample — it was almost entirely the billing module Suchipatra had acquired in 2023, whose engineers had never been told the convention existed. Worse, 84 of the 240 accounts ran on-premises inside hospital data centres and emitted nothing at all; those accounts carried 41 percent of ARR. And in one module a developer had written the patient medical record number into a property called ref, which under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act meant an erasure request now implicated the analytics store itself.

Three weeks later, Rehan Qureshi was looking at a different shape of the same problem. Qureshi had co-founded Nighantu AI, a Bengaluru company whose drafting assistant served in-house legal and compliance teams at 220,000 monthly actives. Week-four retention had slid from 24 percent to 18 percent across two quarters and nobody could say why. The event list had been designed in 2022 for the company's first product, a clause-library search tool: search_performed, clause_copied, document_opened. Those screens no longer existed. The unit of work was now a drafting task running six to forty conversational turns and several tool calls, and no event meant the user got what they came for. On 12 June the team had swapped the underlying model; model_version was present on 41 percent of events, skewed heavily to web, where it had shipped first. Nighantu was spending ₹1.9 crore a quarter on inference it could not attribute to any outcome.

Both had the same tempting answer available: convene the teams, write the canonical list, enforce it. Both were right to hesitate, for opposite reasons. Rao's events were not badly named — most were fine — but they were grained, keyed and populated for a question nobody was asking. Qureshi's product was still changing shape every eight weeks, and a registry written in September would encode a model of the product that was wrong by December.

2. The idea, and the traditions that disagree about it

An event taxonomy is the governed specification of the discrete occurrences a product records for analysis: what each is called, at what grain it fires, which key identifies the actor and the thing acted upon, which properties must travel with it, which timestamp defines when it happened, and who owns it. The name is the smallest of those decisions and the only one most teams argue about.

Two intellectual lineages feed the practice, and they are not the same lineage. The first is dimensional modelling: Ralph Kimball's 1996 treatment of the data warehouse insisted that before you build a fact table you declare the grain — state precisely what one row represents — because every later disagreement about a number is an unnoticed disagreement about grain. The second is the tracking-plan tradition, grown out of web analytics in the 2000s and codified commercially around 2015, most visibly by Segment, in the object-and-past-tense-verb grammar: Order Completed, Report Exported. That tradition gave us the grammar and the governed list; Kimball gave us the thing that makes analyses reconcile. A third, event sourcing, observed that systems already emit authoritative domain events for their own correctness, and that a hand-written analytics layer at the UI will drift from them.

The prescriptive school holds that the event list should be small, curated and enforced at build time, and an unapproved name should fail continuous integration. It will sign: an event whose meaning has not been agreed in advance is not data, it is noise with a timestamp. It will not sign: capture everything now and decide the semantics later. Its evidence is registries that grew to several hundred names of which a minority ever fired.

The schema-on-read school, associated with warehouse-native pipelines, holds that raw events should be captured immutably and meaning constructed downstream in versioned transformation code, where it can be corrected. It will sign: the raw log should be a superset of any question you will later ask. It will not sign: decide in 2025 which questions you will ask in 2028. Its evidence is that every taxonomy eventually needs a semantic change, and only teams who kept the raw payloads could backfill one.

The domain-event school holds that analytics events should be derived from the state transitions the backend already commits, not authored separately at the client. It will sign: if the log says the order was placed and the ledger says it was not, the log is a second, unreliable implementation of the same business logic. It will not sign: product should define the event list independent of the domain model. Its evidence is drift.

The schools agree on the grammar and disagree on when meaning is fixed — at emission, at modelling, or at commit.

3. Mechanics: the five decisions, and the audit that scores them

Experts do not begin with a list of events. They begin with a list of questions, the step most reliably left implicit. Bhide's team wrote 34 questions the renewal model would have to answer — does coder throughput fall before non-renewal? do denial-management adopters churn less? does a clinical champion's departure predict decline? — before proposing a single event. The question list is the specification; the event list implements it. Each event is then a five-part commitment, of which the name is one part.

The formal treatment experts use is a coverage audit, and it is arithmetic rather than anything exotic. A question requires steps, an actor grain and splits. Call it answerable when four conditions hold together: every step has an event; those events carry a key resolvable at the required grain; every split property exists with coverage above a stated threshold and cardinality below a stated ceiling; and the events share consistent time semantics. Coverage is the weighted share of answerable questions, and the weighting is where the method earns its keep.

Across the full 34, nineteen were answerable — unweighted coverage of 56 percent, which Bhide could have presented as "more than half". Weighted by ARR at stake it was 38 percent, because the questions that failed were the expensive ones. That gap is not peculiar to Suchipatra. Taxonomies decay first where the product is least instrumented, and products are least instrumented where deployment is hardest — which in enterprise software is where the largest contracts live. Unweighted coverage systematically flatters the team that computes it.

The second piece of arithmetic concerns silent error. When one action is split across k names and an analyst has probability e of omitting any one, the chance of a correct funnel is (1 − e)k. At Suchipatra, finalising a claim existed under three names with e around 0.15, giving 0.61 — two in five analyses touching that action were wrong, and none raised an error. This is why taxonomy debt is worse than it feels: the failure rate scales with how often the data is used, so damage accelerates exactly as a company becomes more data-literate.

The third piece is the rename tax, the second-order effect teams most often get backwards. Consolidating Suchipatra's three claim events into one broke eleven dashboards, four alert rules and two machine-learning features that read event names directly — nine person-days of repair, plus a discontinuity in every trend chart crossing the cut-over. Leaving them alone cost each analysis twenty minutes of union logic; at forty analyses a quarter that is thirteen person-days a year, forever, with the 39 percent silent error rate on top. Teams hesitate because the rename cost is visible, attributable and lands on one sprint, while the alternative is invisible, distributed, and borne by people who will never connect it to this decision.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims rather than advice.

First: the cost of a bad taxonomy scales with the number of distinct questions asked, not with data volume. Count analyses per quarter. Suchipatra ran roughly 160; Nighantu, with far more rows, ran about 25, because its product team decided by watching session replays. Suchipatra had the stronger case for investment despite the smaller dataset.

Second: taxonomy investment pays only if the core actions are stable over the analysis horizon. Rao's core actions — a claim is coded, submitted, rejected, resubmitted — follow the National Health Authority's workflow and will look the same in 2030. Qureshi's will not; his product's central abstraction changed twice in eighteen months. The claim predicts a deep registry for Suchipatra and a thin durable core plus a permissive experimental tier for Nighantu, which is what each eventually built.

Third: a taxonomy is worth designing only where the data is complete enough to be believed. Suchipatra fails this on 41 percent of ARR. No naming discipline improves an account that emits nothing; the fix belongs in the master services agreement, not the tracking plan.

Fourth: the grain must match the unit the business transacts in. Suchipatra transacts in facilities, Nighantu in completed drafting tasks. Person-grained events were not wrong at either company, only insufficient — and the remedy for insufficiency is an added key, not a rebuild.

The idea becomes actively misleading in three situations. Before product-market fit, a rigid taxonomy encodes yesterday's theory of the product and raises the cost of noticing it was wrong. When governance becomes a proxy for measurement maturity, teams ship an immaculate registry attached to metrics nobody has interrogated — a well-named event feeding a badly chosen North Star is a fast route to a confident mistake. And when review boards block exploratory logging, the organisation loses the mechanism by which it discovers which events were worth having.

5. Hard edges: seams, sensors, regulators and models

The clean account assumes one product, one emission path and one legal regime. Real companies have none of these.

Multi-product companies hit the seam first. Suchipatra's clinical and billing modules both had a claim to the name Document Signed, meaning different things at different grains. Mature teams settle on a namespaced event with a shared core: keys and time semantics are company-wide law, the name carries a product prefix, and only a dozen truly cross-product events are unified. Two-sided products face the mirror problem — a freight load cancelled by a shipper and one cancelled by a carrier are the same occurrence from opposite ends. Two events make every marketplace-wide count an error-prone union; one event with an actor_side property makes every side-specific dashboard a filter. The second is right, and the tell is that any cross-side question needs the join key, not the name.

Regulation changes the taxonomy's contents, not only its handling. Under the DPDP Act, purpose limitation means a property collected to improve clinical documentation cannot be quietly reused to score renewal risk, which forces teams to tag each property with a lawful basis at specification time. Suchipatra's ref property was not a compliance footnote; every erasure request now meant rewriting immutable event partitions. Hardware adds a different constraint: firmware in a municipal pump house may not be updated for five years, so the device's schema is frozen and versioning becomes one-directional — the warehouse must understand version 1 forever, because version 1 will still be transmitting in 2030.

AI-native products break the assumption underneath all of this, that the meaningful unit is an action the user took. At Nighantu it is a task the user and the model completed together; success is inferred rather than observed, and the same input produces different outputs across model versions. That makes model_version, prompt_template_id and tool_calls load-bearing keys rather than optional enrichments: without them on every task event, a whole class of question — did the June model change help? — is permanently unanswerable for the period they were missing.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

Naming disputes are almost always grain disputes wearing a disguise

The tell is a meeting in which two people keep proposing names for the same thing and neither will yield. Underneath, one imagines one row per click and the other one row per completed task. The obvious reading — that this is stylistic — is wrong, and it is why such meetings never resolve on their own. Experts interrupt with "what does one row represent?" and the argument ends in ninety seconds. Kimball's instruction to declare the grain was never really about warehouses.

The identity key is part of the event's definition, not of its plumbing

The tell is two teams who agree on a name and produce different counts: one keyed the event to the cart, the other to the order. Because the names match, no reconciliation process catches it; the numbers simply differ and each team trusts its own. The obvious reading treats keys as an engineering concern delegated downward. Experts write the key into the specification beside the name, and treat a change of key as a change of event.

There are at least three clocks, and the funnel must name one

The tell is a funnel in which step two occasionally precedes step one, or a daily active count that changes after the fact. Client event time, server receipt time and domain commit time diverge, and on Indian mobile networks the divergence is large: a device on an intermittent connection may hold events for days. The obvious reading is that this is a rounding concern. It is not — it decides whether your retention curve is stable, and it forces an explicit settling window.

Most of a taxonomy's value sits in the negative space

The tell is a team that can compute conversion precisely and cannot diagnose it at all. Success events are obvious and get instrumented; failures, rejections, timeouts and abandonments are invisible to whoever wrote the happy path. Suchipatra logged claim submissions but not the payer's rejection reason, so it could see that 27 percent of claims failed and never say why. The obvious reading is that the business cares about successes. It cares about improving them, which needs the denominator's structure.

Events record change; they do not record state, and teams discover this too late

The tell is the question "how many accounts were on the enterprise plan on 3 June last year?" met with silence. Plan tier lived only as a property on events that happened to fire, so accounts quiet that week are simply absent. The obvious reading is that a property is a fact about the world. It is a fact about the world at the moment something else happened. Recovering state needs transition events such as Plan Changed, or a slowly-changing entity table — a choice made at design time.

Never put a judgement into an event name

The tell is an event called Activation Completed or User Engaged. Activation is a definition the company argues about and revises; baked into the log, revising it invalidates history, so teams keep a definition they no longer believe. Events should record what happened; metrics record what the company decided it means. The obvious reading — that naming the important thing makes it visible — is right about attention and wrong about durability. Keep judgement in the semantic layer, where it versions cheaply.

Client-side loss is not noise, it is bias

The tell is a gap between client-reported and server-reported counts that is stable in aggregate but varies by segment. Ad blockers, background-process limits on low-RAM Android devices and dropped connections in tier-three cities remove events non-randomly. Suchipatra's client-side onboarding funnel under-represented exactly the rural hospital users the renewal model most needed to predict. The obvious reading treats this as a completeness problem to tolerate. It is a validity problem: the missing data correlates with the outcome.

Deprecation is harder than creation, so the exit is designed at birth

The tell is a registry with four hundred names of which a quarter still fire. Nobody deletes an event, because nobody can prove no dashboard depends on it. The obvious reading is that an unused event is free. It is not: it is a permanent tax on every analyst who must decide whether it is the one they want, and it is how the union-error arithmetic compounds. Experts attach a sunset rule and a verification alert the day an event ships.

7. What changes by product type and stage, and what does not

Three things do not change: the grammar; the instruction to declare the grain before the name; and the requirement that any two events you wish to sequence share a resolvable key. Claims that consumer and enterprise taxonomy are fundamentally different practices usually turn out, on inspection, to be claims about grain and completeness dressed up as claims about method.

What genuinely differs is the grain the business transacts in and the emission path available. Consumer products are person-grained with near-complete client emission and enormous volume, so the hard problems are identity stitching and cardinality control. B2B and enterprise products transact at the account or facility, so every core event needs an account key from day one and the person-level event is a means rather than an end; enterprise adds deployment constraints, and on-premises is the extreme, where the only honest answer is a telemetry clause in the contract. Platforms and marketplaces are defined by the join key connecting two sides and by volume asymmetry — a freight marketplace may log a thousand carrier actions per shipper action, which makes naive session-level analysis meaningless. Hardware inverts the latency assumptions and freezes schema versions in the field. AI products shift the grain from action to task and make model and prompt lineage required keys.

Stage changes the enforcement mechanism far more than the design. A ten-person company needs a shared document and one person who reads every pull request that adds an event; formality would cost more than the mistakes. Somewhere between fifty and two hundred engineers — the point where no single person reads all the tracking calls — informal discipline stops working and the mechanism must become a schema registry with automated rejection at build time. Beyond that the question is no longer the list but the federation: which decisions are company-wide law, which product-local, and who arbitrates.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

Nighantu AI: re-graining from screen to task. Qureshi's team replaced eleven screen-shaped events with nine task-shaped ones, anchored on Draft Exported, and made task_id and model_version impossible to omit by injecting them in the SDK wrapper rather than trusting callers. In the first full month, 1.42 million tasks were recorded: 61 percent ended in an export, 22 percent were abandoned mid-task, 17 percent ended in a regeneration loop of four or more attempts. The last figure had been invisible under the old taxonomy, was concentrated in a single document type, and accounted for an estimated ₹31 lakh of the quarter's inference spend. The comparison Qureshi wanted — model A against model B across the June switch — he deliberately did not make. On the 41 percent of historical events carrying model_version, model B showed 66 percent task success against model A's 58; but that 41 percent was web-skewed and web users drafted shorter documents. He recorded the number as uninterpretable rather than quoting it.

Nirdeshika sold connected water-quality analysers to municipal utilities — 22,400 devices, many on 2G links where power was intermittent. Events arrived up to eleven days late, 6.1 percent more than 48 hours late. Daily active devices computed at T+1 under-counted by 4.8 percent, and because the late devices sat in the worst-connected districts, the under-count fell exactly where contracts were most at risk. The fix was not a rename: define event_time as the device clock corrected by a server-supplied offset on every payload, declare a fourteen-day settling window before a period is final, and publish two numbers, provisional and settled. Reconciliation error fell from 4.8 percent to 0.3, and the sales team stopped quoting figures that changed afterwards.

Panjika Freight Exchange: the migration that ate fourteen months. The failure is instructive because the team did the analysis well and the execution badly. Panjika, a Gurugram truck-load marketplace, audited its taxonomy in early 2024, correctly concluded that 180 events needed renaming and re-graining, and shipped the change in one release on 5 May with no dual-write, no version property and no mapping table. History either side of the cut-over was not comparable, which alone would have been survivable. What was not survivable was that two production models read event names directly: the ETA model degraded quietly, and a fraud score began flagging legitimate carriers. A take-rate experiment running across the cut-over read out as a 3 percent lift, the change was rolled out nationally, and the real effect — shipper churn in the Nagpur and Coimbatore corridors — cost an estimated ₹3.4 crore before anyone connected it to the migration. Recovery took five months: a name-mapping table, a backfill from retained raw payloads — possible only because someone had insisted on keeping them — and one handbook rule: an event's meaning is immutable; if the meaning changes, the name changes, and both run in parallel for one analysis cycle. The lesson is not that Panjika should have skipped the migration. It is that a taxonomy has consumers its owners cannot see.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Fix meaning at emission, or fix it downstream. The prescriptive position holds that meaning agreed late is meaning never agreed: a permissive raw log becomes an archaeology project, and the modelling layer meant to impose order becomes a thousand lines of conditional logic encoding forgotten history. Its evidence is the number of companies with rich raw data and no trustworthy funnel. The schema-on-read position holds that every taxonomy is eventually wrong and the only recoverable position is a complete raw record; Panjika survived only because the raw payloads existed. It would be wrong if raw capture systematically degraded emission discipline — and there is real evidence it does, since teams who know they can fix it later specify less carefully. Neither side has a clean comparative study; the answer depends on whether your binding constraint is specification effort or future flexibility.

Client or server as the system of record. The server camp points to loss and bias, to the impossibility of auditing client code across app versions in the field, and to the fact that the backend already knows what happened. The client camp answers that the server does not know what the user saw — an impression, a scroll, an abandoned form leave no server trace — and that a server-only taxonomy silently redefines the product as the set of things that hit an API. The compromise neither camp likes: money and state changes server-authored, intent and attention client-authored, joined on a shared key.

Who owns it. Data engineering ownership produces coherent schemas that drift from what product needs to ask; product ownership produces relevant events inconsistently implemented. The emerging answer — a data product manager owning the registry as a product — is asserted more often than evidenced.

The open question. Whether cheap language models dissolve the problem. If unstructured logs can be structured retroactively on demand, the argument for declaring events in advance weakens considerably. Against that: retroactive extraction cannot recover a key that was never written, cannot make a non-deterministic classifier reproducible across reruns, and produces numbers that change when the extracting model changes — a worse version of the problem taxonomies were invented to solve. The field has not settled this.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this writes a good naming convention. Someone who has internalised it does five things differently. They write the question list before the event list and treat coverage against that list, weighted by the value of the decision, as the metric of the work. They ask "what does one row represent?" before anyone proposes a name, and recognise a stalled naming argument as an undeclared grain disagreement. They instrument the failure path in the same sprint as the success path, because they know the diagnosis lives there. They attach an owner, an alert and a sunset date to every event at birth, treating deprecation as the expensive half of the lifecycle. And they can tell you, without looking, which twelve events their company would be blind without, who is paged when each stops firing, and what the coverage of each required key was last week — because they read the raw table, not the dashboard built on it.

12. What each of them decided

Rao did not commission the full registry. She scoped a fourteen-event renewal core, made facility_id a required key enforced at ingest so the acquired module's events would be rejected rather than silently accepted, and added two events the audit had shown to be load-bearing: Role Changed, making champion departure observable, and Claim Rejected with a payer-supplied reason code. She moved onboarding to server-side emission, purged the ref property, and added a lawful-basis tag to every property specification. For the 84 on-premises accounts she accepted that no technical fix existed and took a commercial route: a nightly signed aggregate export negotiated into the master services agreement at renewal, carrying facility-level counts and no person-level data. Weighted coverage was projected at 71 percent by March 2026 — not 100, and she said so to the board.

Qureshi went the other way on scope and the same way on discipline: nine core events at task grain, with task_id and model_version injected by the SDK so no engineer could omit them under deadline; prompt_text deleted; and, deliberately, a permissive lab.* namespace with ninety-day retention, no review and no dashboards, so the experimentation his product still needed would not route around governance. He recorded the June model comparison as unanswerable and moved on.
